paragraphs: I enrolled in the Nagoya University-University of Adelaide Joint Degree Program in Medical Sciences in April 2016, and I was allowed to study at the University of Adelaide in Australia from the beginning of July 2018 to the end of June 2019. It was a graduate program leading to a joint degree with an overseas university, the first of its kind in Japan, and as a third-year graduate student I spent one year in Australia. Australia is a country with which I have had a personal connection for a long time. My parents went there on their honeymoon, and it was also the destination of my very first trip abroad. The impression it made on me then was vivid. I remember being greatly struck, even as a ten-year-old primary school pupil, by seeing the lives of foreigners with my own eyes for the first time, hearing living English, the cultural differences, and the horizon of a vast continent. Adelaide was a city I was visiting for the first time, but I had heard that it is a famous place that ranks near the top of the world's most liveable cities every year. It is the capital of South Australia, which lies even further south within the southern-hemisphere country of Australia, and it has a compact layout in which everything in the city centre can be reached within a 20-minute walk. It is blessed with a Mediterranean climate and is a mild region where one never sees snow throughout the year. My workplace was a new building called the Adelaide Health and Medical Sciences Building (photo). Research institutions, including hospitals, stood side by side in the area, and the University of Adelaide and the University of South Australia lined the neighbourhood, so it felt like a university town. Many international students were enrolled, and I feel that being able to interact with a diverse group of students, mainly from Asia, will be a great asset in the rest of my life. As for my work, I carried on the theme I had at Nagoya University as it was, and under the supervision of Dr. Carmela Ricciardelli (photo), I conducted research on "peritoneal dissemination and the microenvironment of ovarian cancer." At the end of the graduate program, the paper I had refined together with my supervisors at Nagoya University and the University of Adelaide was accepted without problems, and I was able to complete my thesis as my graduation dissertation. One of the most interesting things about Australia is the diversity of its ecology, which stems from its isolated continent. It is said that about 90% of its mammals, reptiles, insects and so on are endemic species found only on the Australian continent, and I could feel this uniqueness in daily life too. In the park I passed through every day on my way to school (photo), I could see a wide variety of birds living there. Wild birds of a size I had only seen in zoos strolled leisurely across the lawn, and there were birds in primary colours such as red and blue, large flocks of white birds with brave yellow-green crests, and birds that announced the dawn with a shrill cry at the same time every morning. There were so many creatures that I never tired of watching them. Besides these, there were red ants, giant snails, and enormous pine trees with their pine cones, and the diversity of its ecosystem is unparalleled in the world. And diversity is just as deeply rooted in the people and culture of this country. Because of its historical background, white people make up the great majority of the population at 80%, but it is a multiethnic nation composed of various peoples, including people of Asian descent and people of Aboriginal origin. And regardless of race, everyone is "super friendly." Once or twice a week, a complete stranger would speak to me. At first I was wary, but it seemed to be a perfectly natural thing to do. They would ask about my background, and when I told them I was Japanese, they would ask even more questions, and then they would begin to tell me earnestly about how they had grown up. I remember this as if it were only yesterday. What I understood through these encounters is that, interestingly, most people pursue their own happiness first and set it as the most important task in their lives. Moreover, most of this was not about work but about activities based on hobbies and family. In the streets, street musicians played ethnic instruments I had never seen, someone staged a demonstration against political distrust, and someone chatted with friends in a cafe. The people passing by were all smiling and somehow looked happy. On Fridays, the town got lively from early afternoon, and many people chatted over beer on the street. Even in the laboratory, people became sparse after 4 p.m., and on Saturdays and Sundays there was almost nobody. It was only one year of living there, but through these experiences I came to think deeply about the diversity of living things and of human beings. In contrast to the Japanese values of respecting the majority and bearing responsibility collectively, in Australia the opinions of the minority are respected and individual actions carry responsibility. It is the idea of valuing the individual, turning back from diversity. While feeling this difference, I noticed that I held preconceptions about how society should be. Then, setting idealism aside, I came to think once more that I should go forward with ambition along the path that only I can take and that I should follow. I realised that through this study abroad I was able to gain an opportunity for growth not only academically but also as a human being. Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to the doctors of my department at the university who gave me this irreplaceable opportunity to study abroad, and to the doctors and staff of the International Affairs Office who gave me great support for my stay. I will make an effort to use this experience to pass on the same kind of experience to the many juniors who aspire to this program and enrol in it in the future.
